lines: On Duolingo you wave with « Jambo! » in Swahili — French works the same way: one magic word opens every door.
French just adds a twist: a casual hello for friends and a polite one for everyone else.

hi / bye, casual (sah-LU) — for friends only
my name is (zhuh mah-PELL) — literally 'I call myself'
how's it going? (sah VAH) — also the answer: ça va!

Bonus: French weather talk is delightfully dramatic. Il fait beau literally means 'it makes beautiful' out there.

items.prompt: First mission in the French realm: a friendly baker waves at you in the morning. On Duolingo you'd say « Jambo! » — what's your best guess in French?
items.hint: One of these literally means 'good day.'
items.explanation: Bonjour (bohn-ZHOOR) = hello / good day — your all-purpose French greeting, just like Jambo.

items.prompt: Let's build your first full French introduction, piece by piece: « Bonjour, je m'appelle Amal. Et toi ? »

steps.text: Start with the greeting: Bonjour (bohn-ZHOOR) — literally 'good day' (bon = good, jour = day).
Add your name: je m'appelle (zhuh mah-PELL) means 'my name is' — literally 'I call myself.' So: Bonjour, je m'appelle Amal.

check.question: What does « je m'appelle » literally mean?

steps.text: Bounce the question back: Et toi ? (ay TWAH) = 'And you?' Now the other person introduces themselves.
All together: « Bonjour, je m'appelle Amal. Et toi ? » — Hello, my name is Amal. And you? That's a real conversation!

items.explanation: À demain = see you tomorrow; à bientôt = see you soon (no exact date). Precision matters for comebacks!

items.explanation: Au revoir = goodbye (literally 'until the re-seeing'); à bientôt = see you soon.

items.hint: Sounds like: sah-LU.

items.prompt:
Legendary: pick the exact translation of this doorway exchange.

« Bonsoir, madame ! Je m'appelle Amal. — Enchantée, Amal ! Ça va ? — Très bien, merci. Au revoir ! — À demain ! »
items.answer: Good evening, ma'am! My name is Amal. — Delighted to meet you, Amal! How are you? — Very well, thanks. Goodbye! — See you tomorrow!
options: Good evening, ma'am! My name is Amal. — Delighted to meet you, Amal! How are you? — Very well, thanks. Goodbye! — See you tomorrow!
Good morning, ma'am! My name is Amal. — Delighted to meet you, Amal! How are you? — So-so, thanks. Goodbye! — See you soon!
Good evening, miss! My name is Amal. — Thank you, Amal! How old are you? — Very well, thanks. Good night! — See you Monday!
Hello, ma'am! My name is Amal. — Delighted, Amal! What's your name? — Very well, thanks. Goodbye! — See you tonight!
items.hint: Check three clues: bonsoir, très bien, à demain.
items.explanation: Bonsoir = good evening, très bien = very well, à demain = see you tomorrow — every clue locks the answer in.

items.prompt: The market baker says you may sample « dix-sept » mini-croissants. You know dix = 10 and sept = 7. Best guess: how many croissants is that?
items.hint: French glues small numbers together with math. Which operation feels right here?
items.explanation: Dix-sept = 10 + 7 = 17. French numbers are tiny addition problems wearing hyphens.

items.prompt: Let's crack the French number machine: build 17, then 25, then the legendary 80 and 90.

steps.text: Teens add onto ten: dix-sept (dees-SET) = 10 + 7 = 17. Same trick for dix-huit (18) and dix-neuf (19). But 11–16 have their own short names: onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize.
Tens + ones snap together with a hyphen: vingt-cinq (van-SANK) = 20 + 5 = 25. The tens to know: vingt 20, trente 30, quarante 40, cinquante 50, soixante 60.
One quirk: numbers ending in 1 (21, 31 … 61) add a tiny 'and': vingt et un = 'twenty AND one' = 21. Everything else keeps the hyphen: vingt-deux, vingt-trois…
Now the famous part. French has no plain word for 70, 80 or 90 — it does MATH instead: soixante-dix = 60 + 10 = 70, and quatre-vingts = 4 × 20 = 80. Yes, 'four twenties.'
Top it off with cent (sahn) = 100. So 99 = quatre-vingt-dix-neuf = 4 × 20 + 10 + 9. French numbers are equations — and you already speak fluent equation.

items.prompt: Decode each French number by finishing its math. Write the final values as digits.
items.hint: Just do the arithmetic each name spells out.
items.explanation: That's the whole secret: the name IS the equation — dix-neuf 19, soixante-dix 70, quatre-vingts 80.

items.hint: Trois sounds like 'trwah' — it's in your bridge vocab.
items.explanation: Trois = 3. Un, deux, trois — one, two, three cats to pet.

items.hint: Cinq sounds like 'sank' — five fingers sank into the dough.
items.explanation: Un 1, quatre 4, cinq 5, sept 7, dix 10 — the building blocks for every bigger number.

items.hint: Sounds like: set.

items.hint: They sound like 'trwah' and 'sank.'
items.explanation: Un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six — 1 through 6, the launch sequence of French counting.

items.prompt: Press play. Which number did you hear?
items.hint: Sounds like: kah-TORZ — one of the special teen names.
items.explanation: Quatorze = 14. The numbers 11–16 get custom names: onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize.

items.prompt: Your knitting pattern calls for 16 stitches in the next row. How do you say 16 in French?
items.hint: 16 is the LAST of the custom teen names — the dix-glue pattern only starts at 17.
items.explanation: Seize (sez) = 16. There's no dix-six — French only starts gluing at dix-sept (17).

items.prompt: The teen machine: 17, 18 and 19 are built as ten-plus. Complete each one.
items.hint: 10 + 7, 10 + 8, 10 + 9 — you just need the words for 7, 8 and 9.
items.explanation: Dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf — ten-seven, ten-eight, ten-nine. Pure addition with hyphens.

items.hint: Teens to watch: douze 12, treize 13, quinze 15, seize 16.
items.explanation: Fast 0–20 recall makes the big composed numbers feel easy — they're just these plus glue.

items.prompt: Which French word means 40?
items.hint: Careful — quatorze is 14! The tens end in -ante.
items.explanation: Quarante = 40; quatorze = 14. The -ante ending marks the tens: trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante.

items.prompt: Match each tens word to its value.
items.hint: Cinquante hides cinq (5) — five tens. Soixante hides six.
items.explanation: 20–60 count up politely: vingt, trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante. The drama starts at 70.

items.prompt: Your K-pop photocard binder holds « vingt-cinq » cards. Type that number in digits.
items.hint: vingt + cinq, glued with a hyphen — add the pieces.
items.explanation: Vingt-cinq = 20 + 5 = 25. Tens plus ones, hyphen included.

items.prompt: Press play. Which number did you hear?
items.hint: Sounds like: tront-TRWAH — a tens word plus a little one.
items.explanation: Trente-trois = 30 + 3 = 33. You can hear the two pieces snap together.

items.prompt: 21 is special — it sneaks in a tiny extra word. Which is the correct French for 21?
items.hint: Numbers ending in 1 say 'twenty AND one' — et means and.
items.explanation: Vingt et un = 21, and the pattern repeats: trente et un (31) … soixante et un (61). Vingt-deux (22) and friends go back to hyphens.

items.prompt: Arrange the words to say 'I am eleven years old' — literally 'I have eleven years.'
items.hint: Start with 'I have' — in French, age is something you HAVE.
items.explanation: J'ai onze ans = I am 11. French speakers have their years like treasure; they don't 'be' them.

items.prompt: The fan site says the K-pop comeback drops in « soixante-dix » days. Decode the math: how many days?
items.hint: soixante = 60, dix = 10. French has no plain word for this number — it adds.
items.explanation: Soixante-dix = 60 + 10 = 70. French skips inventing a word for 70 and just keeps counting past sixty.

items.prompt: Your scarf pattern needs « quatre-vingts » stitches — literally 'four twenties.' Do the multiplication and type the stitch count in digits.
items.hint: quatre × vingt = 4 × 20.
items.explanation: Quatre-vingts = 4 × 20 = 80 — French genuinely multiplies here. (The -s on vingts stays only when no other number follows.)

items.prompt: Press play. Which number did you hear? (It's one of the math-built ones.)
items.hint: Sounds like: swah-sont-KANZ — sixty plus a teen.
items.explanation: Soixante-quinze = 60 + 15 = 75. Past 69, French keeps stacking teens onto soixante.

items.prompt: Decode 92 like a code-breaker. Fill in the two missing pieces (digits).
items.hint: quatre-vingt = four twenties; douze is a teen you know.
items.explanation: Quatre-vingt-douze = 4 × 20 + 12 = 92. Every scary-looking big number falls to this two-step decode.

items.prompt: A market stall lists its number translations. One is wrong — tap it.
items.hint: Run the math on each one: quatre-vingt-dix has a + 10 hiding in it.
items.explanation: Quatre-vingt-dix = 4 × 20 + 10 = 90, not 80. Plain 80 is quatre-vingts.

items.prompt: Arrange the words to announce 'There are eighty croissants.'
items.hint: 'There is / there are' in French is the three-word combo il y a.
items.explanation: Il y a quatre-vingts croissants = there are 80 croissants. Il y a is French's all-purpose 'there is/are.'

items.prompt: Press play, then type the number you hear — in digits.
items.hint: Sounds like: deez-NUF — a ten-plus teen.
items.explanation: Dix-neuf = 10 + 9 = 19.

items.prompt: Legendary: at the wizard market, a spellbook costs « soixante-dix-sept » coins and a cat charm costs « vingt-trois » coins. Decode both numbers, add them, and type the total in digits.
items.hint: 60 + 10 + 7 for the book; 20 + 3 for the charm. Then add.
items.explanation: Soixante-dix-sept = 77 and vingt-trois = 23, so 77 + 23 = 100 — which French calls cent. Magic budget: spent.

items.prompt: You know lundi = Monday, day one of the French week. Explorer's hunch: what does « mardi » mean?
items.hint: The days march in order — mardi comes right after lundi.
items.explanation: Mardi = Tuesday, day two of the week. Fun fact: Mardi Gras literally means 'Fat Tuesday.'

items.prompt: Let's build a full French calendar sentence: today's day, the date, and the weather.

steps.text: The seven days, in French order: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche. The week starts on Monday — and French days are never capitalized.
Say the day: Aujourd'hui, c'est mardi = today is Tuesday. Aujourd'hui (oh-zhoor-DWEE) = today.

check.question: Which day starts the French week?

steps.text: Add the date with le + number + month: le quatorze juillet = July 14, France's national holiday. French says the number BEFORE the month — backwards from English.
One exception: the 1st of a month uses premier (first): le premier mai = May 1st. Every other date uses a plain number.
Finish with weather: Il fait beau = it's lovely out. All together: Aujourd'hui, c'est mardi le quatorze juillet, et il fait beau ! A whole forecast in one breath.

items.prompt: It's Monday, July 14 — finish the journal entry with the French day.
items.hint: Day ONE of the French week — it sounds like luhn-DEE.
items.explanation: Aujourd'hui, c'est lundi = today is Monday. Le quatorze juillet is Bastille Day — fireworks over all of France.

items.prompt: Your Duolingo streak screen says « samedi ». Which day is it?
items.hint: It's a weekend day — sounds like sahm-DEE.
items.explanation: Samedi = Saturday. The weekend pair is samedi and dimanche.

items.prompt: Match each French day to its English day.
items.hint: Lundi launches the week; dimanche closes it.
items.explanation: Lundi, mercredi, vendredi, dimanche — Monday, Wednesday, Friday, Sunday. Notice: no capital letters on French days.

items.prompt: Your cat glares out the window: « Il pleut. » What's the weather?
items.hint: Pleut sounds like 'pluh' — think puddles.
items.explanation: Il pleut = it's raining. Cats and rain: eternal enemies.

items.prompt: Press play. Which day did you hear?
items.hint: Sounds like: luhn-DEE — day one of the French week.
items.explanation: Lundi = Monday, named after la lune (the moon) — moon-day, just like in English!

items.prompt: Your streak calendar got shuffled! Put the days in order, starting with the FIRST day of the French week.
items.hint: French calendars start on Monday, not Sunday.
items.explanation: Lundi through samedi — then dimanche (Sunday) caps the weekend. French weeks launch on Monday.

items.prompt: Arrange the words to say 'Today is October 3rd.'
items.hint: Start with 'today' — and remember, the number comes BEFORE the month.
items.explanation: Aujourd'hui, c'est le trois octobre. French dates flip English: the 3 marches in front of October.

items.prompt: French months are sneaky cognates. Match each one to its English month.
items.hint: Sound them out — most French months almost rhyme with their English twins.
items.explanation: Janvier, avril, août, octobre, décembre — and like days, French months skip the capital letters.

items.prompt: School in France wraps up in « juin », and summer break rolls into the next month. Which month comes right after juin?
items.hint: June and July are the twin J months — juin, then…
items.explanation: Juin (June) → juillet (July), the month of Bastille Day fireworks. Août (August) comes after that.

items.prompt: Your Duolingo monthly-badge shelf shows the whole French year — fill in the two missing months.

items.hint: Month 3 shares its name with a red planet; month 5 sounds like 'meh.'
items.explanation: Mars (March) and mai (May). Twelve months, zero capital letters — très French.

items.prompt: Press play for the forecast. Is it scarf-knitting weather?
items.hint: Sounds like: eel feh FRWAH — brrr.
items.explanation: Il fait froid = it's cold. Absolutely scarf weather — cast on!

items.prompt: Match each French season to its English season.
items.hint: L'hiver sounds shivery (lee-VAIR); l'été is when things get heated.
items.explanation: Le printemps, l'été, l'automne, l'hiver — spring, summer, fall, winter. Été even looks sunny with those accents.

items.prompt: Pack for the trip! Sort each phrase: blazing summer day or snowy winter day?
items.hint: Chaud = hot (think hot chocolate: chocolat chaud); neige = snow.
items.explanation: Chaud, soleil and beau belong to summer; neige and froid are winter's crew.

items.prompt: Press play. Which day did you hear?
items.hint: Sounds like: mair-kruh-DEE — the midweek mouthful.
items.explanation: Mercredi = Wednesday. Many French schools traditionally took a midweek break on mercredi — quelle chance!

items.prompt: Your pen pal asks: « Quel jour sommes-nous ? » What does she want to know?
items.hint: Jour = day — you already know it from bonJOUR.
items.explanation: Quel jour sommes-nous ? = what day is it? (Literally 'what day are we?' — answer: Nous sommes mardi.)

items.prompt: Bastille Day fireworks light up July 14. Which is the correct French date?
items.hint: The formula is le + number + month, in exactly that order.
items.explanation: Le quatorze juillet — le first, number before month. France's national holiday since 1880.

items.prompt: On May 1st, French friends trade lily-of-the-valley flowers for luck. Write 'May 1st' in French — remember, the 1st is the special one.
items.hint: Not 'le un mai' — the 1st uses the word for 'first.'
items.explanation: Le premier mai = May 1st, the only date that uses premier instead of a plain number. The lucky flower is called muguet.

items.prompt: Press play for the announcement. What day and date did you hear?

data.audioText: Aujourd'hui, c'est jeudi le douze mars.

items.hint: Sounds like: zhuh-DEE … DOOZ … MARSS — day, number, month.
items.explanation: Jeudi le douze mars = Thursday, March 12. Douze = 12 and mars = March.

items.prompt: Arrange the words to ask 'What's the weather like today?'

items.prompt: Complete the four-season forecast with the missing weather words.

items.hint: Hot ↔ chaud, it snows ↔ il neige, it rains ↔ il pleut.
items.explanation: Il fait chaud in summer, il neige in winter, il pleut in spring — your full forecast toolkit.

items.prompt: Your cat refuses the door with great drama. Press play on the forecast — what's happening outside?

data.audioText: Il y a du vent et il pleut.

items.hint: Sounds like: eel yah du VON … eel PLUH. Two weather events!
items.explanation: Il y a du vent (it's windy) et il pleut (it's raining) — a two-part storm. Wise cat.

items.prompt: Legendary: the fan club posts the concert details — « Le concert est samedi, le vingt et un juin, le premier jour de l'été. » Decode the FULL announcement.
items.answer: The concert is Saturday, June 21, the first day of summer
options: The concert is Saturday, June 21, the first day of summer
The concert is Sunday, June 21, the first day of July
The concert is Saturday, July 21, the first day of summer
The concert is Saturday, June 1, the last day of spring
items.hint: Three decodes: samedi, vingt et un (20 + 1), juin — then l'été.
items.explanation: Samedi = Saturday, le vingt et un juin = June 21 (that's 20 + 1!), and l'été = summer. June 21 really does open summer — France throws the Fête de la Musique that day.
